Our Father’s world is a world unspoiled by human invention and intervention. While sin and technology have warped and stolen many lovely things from the human race, there abide still a few that remain unmarred by civilization. Little children in the fresh innocence of their unsoiled morning top the ranks as a bit of heaven on earth and call all observers heavenward. Another is the fowl of the air as prescribed in Genesis. Paul pleaded with the Corinthian church, “Doth not nature itself teach you?” We are exhorted to consider the lilies, the ravens, and the grass of the field. Each of these bears a significant dimension of the eternal God in their existence and gives us definition to their Creator. Perhaps all of nature can give us snapshots into heavenly places if we had the time and eyes to observe it.

Birds hold a unique place in God’s creation, for their sphere is in the heavens. Man may mount on the wings of a plane and evade the lower earth for a few hours, but the heavens will never be a place of his common dominion. The birds are a picture of a heavenly race, for they are at home there. They are a natural representation of the saints and angels of God and so we do well to give them due attention. While there may be dozens of lessons to be drawn from these vessels of grace and beauty, one of the most prominent and outstanding virtues will be observed in the song that they raise. Many animals dwelling on the earth are virtually mute. Of the ones that do speak, it is often to threaten or express complaint. “Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? Or loweth the ox over his fodder?” (Job 6:5). When they are happy and content, they have no message to convey. The dog barks at an intruder to drive him away, while the cat mews for attention. They speak when they are threatened or dissatisfied, in fear or in pain. Similarly, the earthly human shares its nature with the mammals of the field.

Birds are diverse. They exercise their joyous vocals so much that they are the epitome of happiness. The expression “happy as a lark” is so common a term that it is used by people who have never even ventured to the meadow to see or hear a lark. While some may inform us that these songs are mere mating calls and have little to do with their feelings, we cannot escape the inner conviction that, whether mating or not, these birds delight in bearing a jubilant expression of joy and we do well to let them teach us. “Is any merry? Let him sing psalms” (James 5:13). The birds do this incessantly and it seems impossible to draw any other conclusion but that they are happy while doing so. Wander near the nest of a swallow and you will find that they have ways of expressing depreciation as well. The killdeer also has no qualms with expressing rash disfavor to those who intrude their domain, but these are not to be mistaken as songs. The singing birds are a beautiful painted picture of the saints and angels of God.

How little knowledge of heaven is committed to our understanding. The scenes of heavens described and laid out before us in Revelations can hardly bring our finite minds into its infinite realm. One dimension that we can connect with is that it is a place filled with singing. Little wonder, for it is the culminating end of the contented and joy-filled saints of God, and there they will sing a new song. Nearly every scene at the throne in Revelations is marked by some dimension of praise. “And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God” (Ps 40:3). On 22 occasions, the Scriptures reiterate the phrase, I will sing.

It is the nature of the birds to sing. It is their waking thought as morning guilds the sky, and it flows from within them like a fountain. Not all of their songs are alike. Some are elaborate in their duration, meter, and pitch, while others are plain. Some merely chirp with a merry heart. The robin opens up the choir in early spring, but his song is soon surpassed in beauty by the song sparrow and again by the rose-breasted grosbeak. The song of the wren trumps them all for longevity and vibrancy. The canary sings in a cage, while the nightingale sings in the dark. The robins sing in the rain. The buntings fill in the heat of the day when other birds are silent. As diverse as their song may be, they all commonly burst forth in exuberant happiness. It is here that they shall instruct us.

“Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). The advent of Christ was marked by the angelic host announcing peace and goodwill toward men. All those who will bear His name must deliver the same tidings. In John 4, we happen upon the scene at Jacob’s well, where Christ asks the woman for a drink. Her reply seems to bear a tinge of bitterness. “Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.” Though she esteemed herself as a spiritual person and willingly followed Him into religious discourse, she had no song. Like the well that they speak over, her water was buried deep below the surface and how laborious the effort to bring it forth. Christ offers another alternative. “But the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:14).

The well of Christ is an artesian well. One needs neither pitcher nor labor to draw it out, for it spews forth abundantly on its own accord. While Christ is probably speaking of the Spirit as in John 7:38, surely this may be just as applicable to a joy-laden heart. What is a more apt outpouring to flow from a Christ-inspired wellspring than the rapture of a song? “Behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart” (Is 65:14). Now this should all seem plain enough to understand and easy enough to do but, alas, we find we have a constant and persistent adversary who seeks to thwart our song. We are not unaware of his devices...

Sin. Not all birds sing. There are some whose visage is black as sin. These only seem to screech and scream and are no example for the saints of God to emulate. The babbling noise we hear emanating from many passing vehicles certainly parallels the songs of such foul fowl. “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird” (Rev 18:2). These abundant creatures are the fallen spirits, the fowls waiting to devour the seed sown by the wayside. Of such are the worthless blackbirds, starlings, and grackles. The crows show themselves also at the roadside, feeding on rotting carcasses. Often you will find them in large numbers feeding themselves on the corn the farmer painstakingly planted for himself. So transgresses the selfish soul in his pursuit of happiness, feeding gleefully on the calamity of another and exploiting their sin. He bears no song, for his day is constantly clouded by the misdeeds of others who cross his path.

Neglect. The cowbird is also black (the female is brown/gray). She will be found sitting on a high vantage, shamelessly calling to her lovers by her shrill screeching. She then has the audacity to lay her egg in another bird’s nest, forcing them to raise her offspring. This is certainly a fitting emblem for a good number of females in our day. Though justified by circumstances, these women care not for their own, but are products of neglect. They have no lullaby to share with their young, for they have escorted them to the nest of another while her mind is preoccupied with work and business. “But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother’s breasts” (Ps 22:9). No doubt that the singing mother can implant copious songs in her infant and set the stage for a happy and hope-filled life. While we may show mercy to a woman in dire circumstances, the major song of modern women bears chords that are but dissident and melancholy. These are stopped-up wells like unto the wells that Isaac found upon his return to Gerar. The Philistines “had filled them with earth” (Gen 26:15). So run the spiritually neglected homes of many families today, who pack their schedules so full of earthly commitments that they have no time to spend an hour in song together. If the birds stopped singing, would they even notice?

Ingratitude. Find a soul bathed in unthankfulness, and you will find a soul without a song. If the canary were to refuse to sing in captivity, few of us would ever have heard his rollicking melody. “We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof. For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion. How shall we sing the LORD’S song in a strange land?” (Ps 137:2-4). God’s people had been instructed by Jeremiah to build houses, plant gardens, and raise families. “… And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer. 29:5-7). But they could see no worth in it. With their eyes fixed upon the dismal scene around them, they lost their song. Israel had within its history a rich tradition of song. Their singing erupted at the passage of the Red Sea in the days of Jehoshaphat and had been known to defeat armies. Earthly discomfort is no excuse to withhold gratitude, for our God reigns, and we are His children. Such were the conditions of the Philippian prison where two jailbirds, Paul and Silas, opened the concert at midnight and rocked the corridors with their joyful singing.

When we open our mouths and stretch our vocals in praise, we enact the grace of God. We join the faithful choir alongside Miriam, Deborah, and Hannah, and blend harmoniously with Moses, David, Paul, and Barnabas. At evening, we sing with our Lord and His disciples after supper, and with legions of angels “giving glory to God in the highest.” If that isn’t enough, perhaps we should consider rising at early dawn and singing with the innumerable hosts of our feathered friends who are thankful for God’s loving providence. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord … And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:16, 23).

ODie Welt unseres Vaters ist eine Welt, die durch menschliche Erfindungen und Eingriffe nicht verdorben ist. Obwohl Sünde und Technik viele liebenswerte Dinge der Menschheit verzerrt und gestohlen haben, gibt es dennoch einige, die von der Zivilisation unberührt geblieben sind. Kleine Kinder in der frischen Unschuld ihres unbefleckten Morgens ragen an der Spitze hervor wie ein Stück Himmel auf Erden und ziehen alle Beobachter himmelwärts. Ein weiteres sind die Vögel des Himmels, wie es in Genesis vorgeschrieben ist. Paulus appellierte an die Gemeinde in Korinth: „Doth not nature itself teach you?“ Wir werden ermahnt, die Lilien, die Raben und das Gras des Feldes zu betrachten. Jedes von diesen trägt eine bedeutende Dimension des ewigen Gottes in seinem Dasein und gibt uns eine Vorstellung von ihrem Schöpfer. Vielleicht kann uns die ganze Natur Schnappschüsse himmlischer Orte liefern, wenn wir nur Zeit und Augen hätten, sie zu beobachten.

Vögel haben einen einzigartigen Platz in Gottes Schöpfung, denn ihr Bereich ist in den Himmeln. Der Mensch mag sich auf die Flügel eines Flugzeugs begeben und für ein paar Stunden der niederen Erde entweichen, doch die Himmel werden niemals ein Ort seiner gewöhnlichen Herrschaft sein. Die Vögel sind ein Bild eines himmlischen Geschlechts, denn dort sind sie zu Hause. Sie sind eine natürliche Darstellung der Heiligen und Engel Gottes, und so tun wir gut daran, ihnen gebührende Aufmerksamkeit zu schenken. Während sich Dutzende von Lektionen aus diesen Gefäßen der Gnade und Schönheit ziehen lassen mögen, wird eine der prominentesten und auffälligsten Tugenden im Gesang deutlich, den sie erheben. Viele Tiere, die auf der Erde leben, sind so gut wie stumm. Von denen, die doch Geräusche von sich geben, ist es oft eine Drohung oder ein Ausdruck des Unmuts. “Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? Or loweth the ox over his fodder?” (Job 6:5). Wenn sie glücklich und zufrieden sind, haben sie keine Botschaft zu übermitteln. Der Hund bellt einen Eindringling an, um ihn zu vertreiben, während die Katze miaut, um Aufmerksamkeit zu erlangen. Sie sprechen, wenn sie bedroht oder unzufrieden sind, in Furcht oder Schmerz. Ebenso teilt der irdische Mensch seine Natur mit den Säugetieren des Feldes.

Vögel sind vielfältig. Sie üben ihre freudigen Gesänge so sehr aus, dass sie die Verkörperung von Glück sind. Der Ausdruck „glücklich wie eine Lerche“ ist ein so geläufiger Begriff, dass er von Menschen gebraucht wird, die nie in die Wiese gegangen sind, um eine Lerche zu sehen oder zu hören. Manche mögen uns zwar sagen, dass diese Lieder bloße Balzrufe seien und wenig mit ihren Gefühlen zu tun hätten, doch können wir uns der inneren Überzeugung nicht entziehen, dass diese Vögel, ob balzend oder nicht, Freude daran haben, einen jubelnden Ausdruck des Frohsinns zu zeigen, und wir tun gut daran, uns von ihnen belehren zu lassen. “Is any merry? Let him sing psalms” (James 5:13). Die Vögel tun dies unaufhörlich, und es erscheint unmöglich, zu einem anderen Schluss zu kommen, als dass sie dabei fröhlich sind. Wandere in die Nähe eines Schwalbennestes, und du wirst feststellen, dass sie auch Wege haben, Missbilligung auszudrücken. Der Killdeer scheut sich ebenfalls nicht, stürmischen Widerwillen gegenüber denen zu zeigen, die in sein Revier eindringen, doch dies ist nicht mit Gesang zu verwechseln. Die singenden Vögel sind ein schön gemaltes Bild der Heiligen und Engel Gottes.

Wie wenig Wissen über den Himmel ist unserem Verstand anvertraut. Die Szenen des Himmels, die uns in der Offenbarung beschrieben und vor Augen gelegt werden, können kaum unseren endlichen Geist in ihr unendliches Reich hineinziehen. Eine Dimension, mit der wir Verbindung herstellen können, ist, dass es ein Ort ist, erfüllt vom Gesang. Kein Wunder, denn es ist das vollendende Ende der zufriedenen und freudenvollen Heiligen Gottes, und dort werden sie ein neues Lied singen. Fast jede Szene am Thron in der Offenbarung ist von irgendeiner Form des Lobes geprägt. “And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God” (Ps 40:3). In 22 Stellen wiederholt die Schrift die Wendung, I will sing.

Es liegt in der Natur der Vögel zu singen. Es ist ihr erster Gedanke beim Erwachen, wenn der Morgen den Himmel vergoldet, und es fließt aus ihnen wie eine Quelle. Nicht alle ihre Lieder sind gleich. Einige sind in Dauer, Metrum und Tonhöhe ausgearbeitet, während andere schlicht sind. Einige zwitschern lediglich mit fröhlichem Herzen. Die Amsel eröffnet den Chor im frühen Frühling, doch ihr Gesang wird schnell in Schönheit übertroffen vom Song Sparrow und wieder vom Rose-breasted Grosbeak. Der Gesang der Zaunkönige übertrumpft sie alle an Länge und Lebendigkeit. Die Kanarienvögel singen im Käfig, während die Nachtigall im Dunkeln singt. Die Rotkehlchen singen im Regen. Die Buntings füllen die Hitze des Tages aus, wenn andere Vögel still sind. So vielfältig ihr Gesang auch sein mag, so brechen sie doch alle gemeinschaftlich in überschwängliche Fröhlichkeit aus. Hier werden sie uns unterweisen.

“Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). Das Kommen Christi war von der engelsgleichen Schar begleitet, die Frieden und Wohlwollen den Menschen verkündete. Alle, die Seinen Namen tragen, müssen dieselben Botschaften überbringen. In Johannes 4 begegnen wir der Szene am Jakobsbrunnen, wo Christus die Frau um Wasser bittet. Ihre Antwort scheint einen Hauch von Bitterkeit zu tragen. „Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.“ Obwohl sie sich selbst als eine fromme Person betrachtete und bereitwillig mit ihm in religiöse Gespräche eintrat, hatte sie kein Lied. Wie der Brunnensprung, über den sie sprechen, war ihr Wasser tief unter der Oberfläche vergraben, und wie mühsam war die Anstrengung, es hervorzubringen. Christus bietet eine andere Alternative an. “But the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:14).

Der Brunnen Christi ist ein artesischer Brunnen. Man braucht weder Krug noch Mühe, um ihn zu schöpfen, denn er sprudelt von selbst reichlich hervor. Während Christus wahrscheinlich vom Geist spricht, wie in John 7:38, gilt dies gewiss ebenso gut für ein freudenvolles Herz. Was wäre eine treffendere Ausströmung aus einer von Christus inspirierten Quelle als das Entzücken eines Liedes? “Behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart” (Is 65:14). Nun sollte all dies recht einfach zu verstehen und leicht zu tun sein, doch ach, wir finden, dass wir einen beständigen und hartnäckigen Widersacher haben, der unser Lied zu vereiteln sucht. Wir sind seiner Kunstgriffe nicht unkundig...

Sünde. Nicht alle Vögel singen. Es gibt einige, deren Antlitz so schwarz ist wie die Sünde. Diese scheinen nur zu kreischen und zu schreien und sind kein Vorbild für die Heiligen Gottes. Das schwatzende Getöse, das wir aus vielen vorbeifahrenden Fahrzeugen vernehmen, entspricht gewiss den Liedern solcher üblen Vögel. “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird” (Rev 18:2). Diese zahlreich vorkommenden Kreaturen sind die gefallenen Geister, die Vögel, die darauf warten, den am Wege gesäten Same zu verschlingen. Zu solchen gehören die wertlosen Amseln, Stare und Grackeln. Die Krähen zeigen sich ebenfalls an der Straße, ernähren sich von verwesenden Aas. Oft findet man sie zahlreich, wie sie sich am Mais gütlich tun, den der Bauer mühsam für sich gepflanzt hat. So übertritt die eigensüchtige Seele in ihrem Streben nach Glück, indem sie sich fröhlich an der Not eines anderen labt und dessen Sünde ausnutzt. Sie hat kein Lied, denn ihr Tag ist beständig von den Missetaten anderer getrübt, die ihren Weg kreuzen.

Vernachlässigung. Der Kuhstärling ist ebenfalls dunkel (das Weibchen ist braun/grau). Man findet sie auf hoher Warte sitzen, schamlos ihre Liebhaber mit schrillem Kreischen rufend. Dann hat sie die Frechheit, ihr Ei in das Nest eines anderen Vogels zu legen und zwingt damit diesen, ihren Nachwuchs aufzuziehen. Dies ist gewiss ein treffendes Sinnbild für eine nicht geringe Zahl von Frauen unserer Zeit. Obwohl durch Umstände gerechtfertigt, kümmern sich diese Frauen nicht um ihre Eigenen, sondern sind Produkte der Vernachlässigung. Sie haben kein Schlaflied für ihre Jungen, denn sie haben sie ins Nest eines anderen geleitet, während ihr Geist mit Arbeit und Geschäftigkeit beschäftigt ist. “But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother’s breasts” (Ps 22:9). Zweifellos kann die singende Mutter ihrem Säugling reichlich Lieder einprägen und die Grundlage für ein glückliches und hoffnungsvolles Leben legen. Während wir einer Frau in verzweifelter Lage Barmherzigkeit erweisen mögen, trägt das Hauptlied moderner Frauen Akkorde, die nur dissident und melancholisch sind. Dies sind verstopfte Brunnen wie die Brunnen, die Isaak bei seiner Rückkehr nach Gerar fand. Die Philister „had filled them with earth“ (Gen 26:15). So laufen die geistlich vernachlässigten Heime vieler Familien heute, die ihren Terminkalender so vollpacken mit irdischen Verpflichtungen, dass sie keine Zeit finden, eine Stunde gemeinsam im Gesang zu verbringen. Wenn die Vögel aufhörten zu singen, würden sie es überhaupt bemerken?

Undankbarkeit. Finde eine Seele, die in Undankbarkeit getränkt ist, und du wirst eine Seele ohne Lied finden. Würde der Kanarienvogel sich im Käfig weigern zu singen, hätten nur wenige von uns jemals seine ausgelassene Melodie gehört. “We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof. For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion. How shall we sing the LORD’S song in a strange land?” (Ps 137:2-4). Gottes Volk war von Jeremia angewiesen worden, Häuser zu bauen, Gärten anzulegen und Familien aufzuziehen. „… And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer. 29:5-7). Doch sie konnten darin keinen Wert sehen. Mit den Augen auf die trübe Szenerie um sie gerichtet, verloren sie ihr Lied. Israel hatte in seiner Geschichte eine reiche Liedtradition. Ihr Gesang brach bei der Durchquerung des Roten Meeres aus in den Tagen Joschafat und war dafür bekannt, Heere zu besiegen. Irdischer Unbehagen ist keine Entschuldigung, Dankbarkeit zurückzuhalten, denn unser Gott regiert, und wir sind Seine Kinder. So waren die Bedingungen im Gefängnis von Philippi, wo zwei Gefangene, Paulus und Silas, das Konzert zur Mitternacht eröffneten und die Gänge mit ihrem freudigen Gesang erschütterten.

Wenn wir unsere Münder öffnen und unsere Stimmen zum Lob erheben, vollziehen wir die Gnade Gottes. Wir schließen uns dem treuen Chor neben Mirjam, Debora und Hanna an und mischen uns harmonisch mit Mose, David, Paulus und Barnabas. Am Abend singen wir mit unserem Herrn und seinen Jüngern nach dem Abendmahl und mit Legionen von Engeln, die „giving glory to God in the highest.“ Wenn das nicht genug ist, sollten wir vielleicht erwägen, im frühen Morgengrauen aufzustehen und mit den unzähligen Scharen unserer gefiederten Freunde zu singen, die dankbar sind für Gottes liebevolle Vorsehung. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord … And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:16, 23).

I can still smell the tantalizing cacophony of odors as I clutched my father’s strong hand, weaving our way through the masses of tourists that crowded the building. The vendors at the Green Dragon Farmer’s Market in Ephrata, PA, were trying their best to entice buyers with their rows of fresh fish over ice, cheeses of every variety, deli meat and sandwiches, and piles of fresh fruit. And, oh, the candy! My young preschool mind had never seen so many delectable sweets in one place at one time.

The past two days for me were like the boy at the candy store. I had the privilege of attending Christian Aid Ministries’ first Annual Writers’ Conference. I brushed shoulders with well-known authors such as Katrina Hoover Lee, Johnny Miller, and Ruthann Stelfox. I chatted with aspiring writers and seasoned school teachers. I had the opportunity to sit under hours of inspirational and educational workshops on how to write to communicate, using realistic dialog, descriptive writing, and much more. We all had one common goal in mind. Together, we share and learn how to effectively communicate what is in our hearts, and through the power of the written word, transmit those thoughts to your hearts.

The Heartbeat of the Remnant is a means to communicate inspirational thoughts to eager readers scattered across the globe. Courageous writers step forward with pen and paper or keyboard and monitor and help spread the Good News of the Word of God with caution, correction, and edification. Yet, we need more such writers. We need young believers who bravely submit their first children’s stories. Seasoned grandfathers who bring words of admonishment to the younger generation. Mothers who share experiences and trials with other mothers who are in the throes of raising little ones. Youth encouraging fellow youth to press toward the mark of the prize of the high calling in Christ Jesus. Fathers who with a concerned eye watch the world pressing in on the Christian homes. Together, these aspiring writers will produce a periodical that will endure on the family coffee table for many years. I encourage you, fellow believers, to give it a try. Nelson Mandela, former president of South Africa wrote, “Failure is a teacher, and at the end of your life, what do you think you’ll feel worst about, failing or never trying?”

The Berean Voice has a goal to provide printed material that will help readers navigate through the varied and difficult seasons of life. All our material is available at no charge, but we are dependent on the donations of our supporters. Here is a list of books we have available:

The Power of the Love of Truth
Christian Counseling- Counterfeit?
The Heart of God
Free Indeed!
Pilgrims and Politics
Cup & Cross
The High Cost of Holistic Healing
Secrets of Successful Writing
The Catholic Connection
Psychiatry and Mood altering Medications
The Mennonite Church and Modernism

In 2017 and 2018, the Berean Voice printed a series of vaccine articles in The Heartbeat of the Remnant magazine. These articles were a sincere effort to examine various aspects of vaccine usage with an unbiased approach. We attempted to present the facts as clearly as possible and let the readers draw their own conclusions.

Since then, we have received numerous requests from our readers to publish all the vaccine articles in a booklet, which we agreed to do. But then along came 2019, bringing coronavirus with it. This monumental event upended the vaccine debate and ushered in a frenzied rush to market COVID-19 remedies, many of which were not properly tested. We put the printing on hold, unsure whether to include information on these new and unproven COVID-19 “vaccines.” As time progressed and the deadly nature of COVID-19 abated, we decided to publish the original vaccine articles in a booklet without any additional articles on the COVID-19 debate. We are pleased that the project is nearing completion and will be announced when it is released.

Blessings to all,

Edward Martin

Fri på riktigt!

Den höga kostnaden för holistisk healing

Psykiatri och humörpåverkande mediciner

Sedan dess har vi fått en mängd förfrågningar från våra läsare att publicera alla vaccinationsartiklarna i ett häfte, vilket vi gick med på att göra. Men så kom 2019 och förde med sig coronaviruset. Denna monumentala händelse ställde vaccin-debatten på ända och inledde en febril kapplöpning för att få fram COVID-19-åtgärder på marknaden, många av vilka inte var ordentligt testade. Vi satte tryckningen på vänt, osäkra på om vi skulle inkludera information om dessa nya och obekräftade COVID-19 "vacciner." När tiden gick och COVID-19:s dödliga natur avtagit, bestämde vi oss för att publicera de ursprungliga vaccinationsartiklarna i ett häfte utan några ytterligare artiklar om COVID-19-debatten. Välsignelser till er alla,

“Dr. Waldron, Elsie needs help!” Elsie’s husband was adamant, almost angry, as he stared at me. On the other hand, Elsie stared at the floor, almost as though she wasn’t present. I had never met either of the couple before and was struggling just a little to figure out what was needed from me to help her.

“What is going on?” I asked as I flipped through her chart. This was still in the days of paper charts, and I headed to the lab section of her chart. There wasn’t anything too crazy that I could see there—her liver enzymes were a little elevated, but otherwise, everything seemed OK.

“It’s her drinking!” Her husband told me. “She is drinking more and more every night. She won’t go out except to get whiskey. She drinks till she passes out every night and has to have something every morning to get her started.”

“Is that true?” I asked Elsie, feeling like a judge overseeing a jury trial.

“Yes,” she said. Her face was emotionless, and I couldn’t tell if she wanted to be there or not.

“Do you want help?” I asked her. This was a loaded question. Many people who struggle with alcoholism aren’t ready to break free from its vice-like hold on them. Maybe Elsie was different.

“I guess so,” she said, indifferently. Once again, I couldn’t tell whether she wanted to be there or not.

“At the rate at which you are drinking, you will kill yourself within a year – maybe two at best – if you don’t give up alcohol entirely,” I told her. “If you want to, I will try to find you an inpatient program to detox you and get you off of alcohol.”

“She’s ready,” he husband said firmly.

When dealing with someone who drinks heavily, it is crucial that they don’t simply stop drinking without medical support. Abrupt cessation of alcohol use causes the body to go into withdrawal which can produce a state called Delirium Tremens and even seizures.

I stepped out of the exam room and to make phone calls. It is never easy to find a place for someone to attempt to rehabilitate from any kind of substances, and it was over an hour and a half before I found a facility that was willing to take Elsie and try to help her get off of the whiskey.

I sighed as I reentered her exam room. I had been afraid that I wouldn’t find anywhere for her to go.

I told them about the plan, and her husband nodded vigorously, while Elise continued to stare silently at the floor. “Can we pray together before you go?” I asked them, and when they nodded assent, I prayed with them, asking for freedom and Jesus’ presence in both of their lives.

They left my office with marching orders and directions on where to go. I had a happy glow about me for the rest of the morning, knowing that I had gone the extra mile and had really made a difference in this middle-aged couple’s life.

Around 2 pm, I got a call from the rehab facility. They hadn’t seen even a shadow of Elsie or her husband, which was surprising, since it was a bright sunny day and the facility wasn’t that far away. With a sinking feeling, I dialed the couple’s phone number.

“She won’t go!” Her husband told me. “She tells me that she told me this ahead of time. She’ll try to cut back, but she isn’t willing to go into a rehab facility or any such thing. I guess just tell them that we’ll let them know if she changes her mind.”

My nurse called the rehab facility and told them the bad news, and I sat down in my chair, stunned. What else could I have done? Was there a solution for Elsie—something different that I could have said that would have made a difference in her life?

About a year later, I received the sad news that Elsie had died at home. I was certain that things would have been different if she had gone to rehab and if she had given control to Jesus. None of that had happened, and I felt cynicism pushing into my heart.

Cynicism

We live in an age of cynicism. In ancient Greece, the cynics were an odd assortment of men who specialized in being grouchy and saying mean (they would have said truthful) things to people. They often dressed in rags and behaved in such a way that most of the polite Athenians did not want to be close to them.

Today, cynicism means a tendency to believe the worst about people and circumstances. Cynical people believe that all people are motivated purely by selfishness and that bad events will tend to prevail.

Many young doctors are idealistic and very hopeful. They believe that if they exert the utmost effort, they can make a real, positive impact on their patient’s lives. Unfortunately, as time goes by and they try their hardest and their patients don’t change, they can give up. These doctors still try, but they no longer really hope that their efforts will make much of a difference.

It seems as though people who get involved with politics often have the best of intentions. They see this as a path to changing society for the better. Unfortunately, as time goes by and the faces in charge change, the policies don’t really change, they tend to become cynical.

Sometimes this cynicism is directed against all politicians. Sometimes it is only anger directed against members of the party that opposes their party’s positions. Hope is replaced by cynicism.

Cynicism in the Bible

If there is a book in the Bible that seems to have been written by a cynical man, it is the book of Ecclesiastes. The Preacher, who we understand to be Solomon, lists all of the things that he endeavored in an attempt to find joy.

In chapter 2:17-23 Solomon describes work as futile. He finishes by saying, “For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 2:22,23)

He saw the world as being dominated by tyrants and there was little that the people could do about it. Solomon went so far as to say that political power was meaningless “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

In Ecclesiastes 6:6, he seems to disparage long life. “Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?”

Of course, he finishes his short book with the instruction to remember our Creator in the days of our youth. There is a blessing for those who choose to focus on God when they have a little bit of energy left and not, when they are old and jaded, like Solomon.

Later on, it almost seemed as though God had given up on His people. He still sent prophets to them, but He knew without a doubt that the people would refuse to respond. “Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee” (Jeremiah 7:27).

Even in the New Testament, Paul told Timothy that the time was coming when people would no longer listen to sound doctrine. “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;” (2 Timothy 4:3).

By picking and choosing these passages, we can come away with a very gloomy view of the future and, more specifically, of human’s willingness to change. It seems there is little point of investing ourselves in the people around us. They are full of woe and are as likely to change as a chipmunk is to master differential calculus.

The Opposite of Cynicism

The opposite of cynicism is hope. It is the belief that the future could be better.

It is interesting that the Apostle Paul spoke of tribulations in the Epistle to the Romans, “And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:3-5).

We may not have reached the place where we glory in the trials we experience, but certainly, they should bring us these other things that he mentions. For, we grow in patience and experience, even as we deal with trials, but more than that, we come to realize that we have hope for tomorrow because we serve a great God.

The contrast in the story of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15 teaches us much about hope. The father and the older brother were strikingly different in their attitudes.

The father had never given up hope – he knew that his son had failed him and gone far from what he knew was right and yet, the father still desired to see the prodigal come to himself and return home.

On the other hand, the older brother not only had no hope for his younger brother, but he was also angry with him. The prodigal had wasted his money, he had lived in sin, and now, he had returned home just because he was out of money.

Certainly, there was no reason to trust the younger son. Yet, that is exactly what our Heavenly Father does for us.

Look for Hope in the Right Places

Part of the problem is that we look for hope in the wrong places. A number of years ago, a presidential candidate ran for office under the slogan “Hope and Change,” and yet, even though he was elected, I imagine most folks did not feel that their lives were significantly changed for the better.

Pursuing the things this world values—political power and wealth is guaranteed to bring emptiness. This is Satan’s pattern—he always over-promises and under-delivers.

This was what he did when he tempted Jesus, “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8). All of the things Satan offered, nothing compared with the glory that Jesus eventually received from the road that led to the cross.

In the same way, Satan would like to distract Christians from seeking the things that are valuable, and that will bring hope. Satan tells Christians that politics will not only change the world for the better, it is an easier way to change the world.

The Bible is clear that we build hope as we nurture our relationship with God and then work to help our brothers and sisters build that same relationship in their own lives. The reason that we can hope is not because people are so wonderful—we don’t have to live very long to realize that they aren’t. The reason we hope is because we serve an awesome, faithful God who walks with us through the worst of our trials.

Remember that We Have Undeserved Hope

Jesus’ messages about forgiveness make it clear that one of the major reasons that we have for forgiving others in our lives is that we have received great and undeserved forgiveness. The same is true for hope.

Each one of us was hopeless and without reason to expect to receive hope and we were still given a ray of light in the midst of our darkness. Maybe part of the reason that we have so much trouble hoping for good things for the people around us is that we do not remember how hopeless we were before we found grace.

If Jesus was able to bring hope to our hopeless existence, then certainly He can do wonderful things in the hearts and lives of others around us. The only people we should give up on are the ones that our Savior has given up on as well.

Small Efforts Do Make a Difference

I remember having a conversation with a young person who was planning to go into medicine and had a plan to go to a foreign country and serve the people there. As we were talking, an older man entered the conversation and shared that he saw little hope for change in developing countries.

The people in those countries just weren’t interested in getting better and didn’t do the minimum necessary to stave off things like worms and parasites. Doctors and nurses couldn’t make a difference in such an environment.

I could sense the heart of the youth sinking as this older man shared. He had experience, and he had given up hope. The sad thing was that he was also stealing the hope of someone who still had a desire to serve.

When I was in training, I had a surgeon tell me that family doctors didn’t really do anything. They simply kept their patients alive till their next office visit, whereas surgeons really “fixed” people—taking out (or off) the offending body part.

At the end of the day, small efforts do make a difference. I don’t do brain surgery, but I still can make a difference in someone else’s life— maybe just by spending a little time and listening and praying. This is true for all of us.

More than that, we come to realize that making this effort changes our own lives for the better. Jesus told the sheep that as they ministered to “the least of these my brethren,” they were ministering to Him.

Even if no one’s life is improved, our Savior knows our desires and feels our efforts, and will reward them someday.

A Few Things to Remember

When we face failures, we tend to move in one of two directions. Those of us who are optimists tend to believe that this episode was an isolated event and that the future is still bright. On the other hand, pessimists believe that failures are permanent, personal, and pervasive.

Pessimists believe that their failures are the result of intrinsic character flaws that they have and that these things affect all of their lives and are unlikely to change. Unlike the righteous man who falls to rise again, these people fall and lie where they fall, defeated at the outset.

When we are dealing with other people, we need to give them the same grace that we should give ourselves. They, too, are growing, and if they have a failure today, they will do better tomorrow. Maybe they will fail again, but they will at least “fail better.”

Conclusion

Cynicism is rife in our world. Many have given up hope for a better future, and it is understandable for those who have invested their hope in this world’s institutions. There is no real hope in government or in armies or in bureaucracy.

The song says, “Oh to have no hope in Jesus, how dark this world must be!” For, Jesus is the one who brings light into our darkness and allows us to continue, even when others fail us.

God is the one who redeems us. He is the one who sent the prophets, even though their messages were ignored, and the prophets were persecuted. He is the one who continues to hope for us, even when we have failed Him so many times in the past.

He is the reason we carry on. He is the reason that we have hope, not only for ourselves but also for our brothers.

“Dott. Waldron, Elsie ha bisogno d’aiuto!” Il marito di Elsie era risoluto, quasi arrabbiato, mentre mi fissava. Dall’altra parte, Elsie guardava per terra, come se non fosse davvero presente. Non avevo mai incontrato nessuno dei due prima d’ora e stavo lottando un po’ per capire cosa si aspettassero da me per aiutarla.

“Che succede?” chiesi sfogliando la sua cartella. Erano ancora i tempi delle cartelle cartacee, e andai alla sezione degli esami di laboratorio. Non vedevo nulla di particolarmente anomalo lì: gli enzimi epatici erano un po’ elevati, ma per il resto tutto sembrava a posto.

“È per il suo bere!” mi disse il marito. “Beve sempre di più ogni sera. Non esce se non per comprarsi il whisky. Beve finché non sviene ogni notte e la mattina ha bisogno di qualcosa per cominciare.”

“È vero?” chiesi a Elsie, sentendomi come un giudice che sovrintende a una giuria.

“Sì,” disse. Il suo volto era inespressivo e non riuscivo a capire se volesse essere lì o no.

“Vuoi aiuto?” le chiesi. Era una domanda carica. Molte persone che lottano con l’alcolismo non sono pronte a liberarsi dalla morsa che li stringe. Forse Elsie era diversa.

“Immagino di sì,” rispose, con indifferenza. Anche in questo caso non capivo se volesse essere lì o no.

“Con il ritmo con cui bevi, ti ucciderai entro un anno – forse due al massimo – se non smetti completamente di bere,” le dissi. “Se vuoi, cercherò per te un programma di ricovero per disintossicarti e allontanarti dall’alcol.”

“È pronta,” disse con fermezza il marito.

Quando si tratta di qualcuno che beve molto, è fondamentale che non smetta semplicemente senza supporto medico. La sospensione brusca dell’uso di alcol fa entrare il corpo in astinenza, che può produrre uno stato chiamato Delirium Tremens e persino convulsioni.

Uscii dalla sala visita per fare delle telefonate. Non è mai facile trovare un posto dove qualcuno possa tentare di riabilitarsi da qualunque sostanza, e passarono più di un’ora e mezza prima che trovassi una struttura disposta a prendere Elsie e provare ad aiutarla a smettere col whisky.

Sospirai mentre rientravo in sala visita. Temevo di non aver trovato alcun posto dove farla andare.

Raccontai loro del piano, e il marito annuì vigorosamente, mentre Elsie continuava a fissare silenziosa il pavimento. “Possiamo pregare insieme prima che te ne vada?” chiesi, e quando acconsentirono, pregai con loro, chiedendo libertà e la presenza di Gesù nelle loro vite.

Uscirono dal mio studio con ordini e indicazioni su dove recarsi. Ebbi una sensazione di soddisfazione per il resto della mattinata, sapendo di aver fatto uno sforzo in più e di aver davvero fatto la differenza nella vita di questa coppia di mezza età.

Verso le 2 del pomeriggio ricevetti una chiamata dalla struttura di riabilitazione. Non avevano visto nemmeno un’ombra di Elsie o di suo marito, cosa sorprendente, dato che era una giornata di sole e la struttura non era così lontana. Con un senso di sconforto chiamai il numero della coppia.

“Non vuole andare!” mi disse il marito. “Dice che me l’aveva detto prima. Proverà a ridurre il bere, ma non è disposta ad andare in una struttura o in qualcosa del genere. Immagino che possiamo dirgli che li avviseremo se cambia idea.”

La mia infermiera chiamò la struttura e diede la cattiva notizia, e io mi sedetti sulla mia sedia, stupefatto. Cos’altro avrei potuto fare? C’era una soluzione per Elsie—qualcosa di diverso che avrei potuto dire che avrebbe cambiato la sua vita?

Circa un anno dopo ricevetti la triste notizia che Elsie era morta a casa. Ero convinto che le cose sarebbero andate diversamente se fosse andata in riabilitazione e se avesse affidato il controllo a Gesù. Niente di tutto ciò era accaduto, e sentii il cinismo insinuarsi nel mio cuore.

Cinismo

Viviamo in un’epoca di cinismo. Nell’antica Grecia, i cinici erano un assortimento strano di uomini specializzati nell’essere scontrosi e nel dire cose cattive (avrebbero detto veritiere) alla gente. Spesso si vestivano di stracci e si comportavano in modo tale che la maggior parte degli ateniesi educati non voleva stare loro vicino.

Oggi il cinismo significa una tendenza a credere il peggio delle persone e delle circostanze. I cinici credono che tutte le persone siano mosse esclusivamente dall’interesse personale e che gli eventi negativi tenderanno a prevalere.

Molti giovani medici sono idealisti e molto speranzosi. Credono che se si impegnano al massimo, possono avere un impatto reale e positivo sulla vita dei loro pazienti. Sfortunatamente, col passare del tempo e nonostante i loro sforzi i pazienti non cambino, possono arrendersi. Questi medici continuano a provarci, ma non sperano più davvero che i loro sforzi faranno molta differenza.

Sembrerebbe che le persone coinvolte nella politica spesso abbiano le migliori intenzioni. Vedono in essa una via per cambiare la società in meglio. Purtroppo, col passare del tempo e col cambiare delle persone al potere, le politiche non cambiano davvero e tendono a diventare cinici.

A volte questo cinismo è diretto contro tutti i politici. A volte è soltanto rabbia verso membri del partito opposto. La speranza è sostituita dal cinismo.

Il cinismo nella Bibbia

Se c’è un libro nella Bibbia che sembra scritto da un uomo cinico, è il libro dell’Ecclesiaste. Il Predicatore, che comprendiamo essere Salomone, elenca tutte le cose in cui si è impegnato nel tentativo di trovare gioia.

Nel capitolo 2:17-23 Salomone descrive il lavoro come futile. Conclude dicendo: “For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 2:22,23)

Vide il mondo dominato da tiranni e c’era poco che le persone potessero fare al riguardo. Salomone arrivò a dire che il potere politico era privo di senso: “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

In Ecclesiaste 6:6 sembra disprezzare la lunga vita. “Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?”

Certo, conclude il suo breve libro con l’istruzione di ricordare il nostro Creatore nei giorni della nostra giovinezza. C’è una benedizione per coloro che scelgono di concentrarsi su Dio quando hanno ancora un po’ di energia e non quando sono vecchi e disincantati, come Salomone.

Più tardi, sembra quasi che Dio avesse abbandonato il Suo popolo. Continuò a mandare profeti, ma sapeva senza dubbio che il popolo avrebbe rifiutato di rispondere. “Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee” (Jeremiah 7:27).

Anche nel Nuovo Testamento, Paolo disse a Timoteo che sarebbe venuto un tempo in cui le persone non avrebbero ascoltato la sana dottrina. “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;” (2 Timothy 4:3).

Scegliendo e scegliendo questi passi, si può rimanere con una visione molto cupa del futuro e, più specificamente, della volontà degli uomini di cambiare. Sembra che valga poco investire nelle persone intorno a noi. Sono piene di guai e sono tanto propense a cambiare quanto uno scoiattolo ad approcciarsi al calcolo differenziale.

Il contrario del cinismo

Il contrario del cinismo è la speranza. È la convinzione che il futuro potrebbe essere migliore.

È interessante che l’apostolo Paolo parli delle tribolazioni nell’Epistola ai Romani: “And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:3-5).

Potremmo non essere ancora arrivati al punto di glorificarci nelle prove che viviamo, ma certamente esse dovrebbero portarci le altre cose che egli menziona. Cresciamo infatti nella pazienza e nell’esperienza mentre affrontiamo le prove, ma, più ancora, arriviamo a comprendere che abbiamo speranza per il domani perché serviamo un grande Dio.

Il contrasto nella storia del Figliol Prodigo in Luca 15 ci insegna molto sulla speranza. Il padre e il fratello maggiore avevano atteggiamenti sorprendentemente diversi.

Il padre non aveva mai perso la speranza: sapeva che il figlio lo aveva deluso e si era allontanato da ciò che sapeva essere giusto e, tuttavia, il padre desiderava ancora che il prodigo tornasse in sé e rientrasse a casa.

D’altra parte, il fratello maggiore non solo non nutriva speranza per il fratello minore, ma era anche arrabbiato con lui. Il prodigo aveva sperperato i suoi soldi, aveva vissuto nel peccato e ora era tornato a casa solo perché era rimasto senza denaro.

Sicuramente non c’era motivo di fidarsi del figlio minore. Eppure, è esattamente quello che il nostro Padre celeste fa per noi.

Cerca la speranza nei posti giusti

Parte del problema è che cerchiamo la speranza nei posti sbagliati. Alcuni anni fa un candidato presidenziale si candidò con lo slogan “Hope and Change” e, anche se fu eletto, immagino che la maggior parte della gente non abbia sentito che le proprie vite fossero significativamente cambiate in meglio.

Perseguire le cose che questo mondo valorizza—il potere politico e la ricchezza—porta certamente al vuoto. Questo è lo schema di Satana—promette sempre troppo e mantiene poco.

Questo è quello che fece quando tentò Gesù: “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8). Tutte le cose che Satana offrì non si paragonavano alla gloria che Gesù ricevette infine dalla strada che portava alla croce.

Allo stesso modo, Satana vorrebbe distrarre i cristiani dal cercare le cose che sono preziose e che portano speranza. Dice ai cristiani che la politica non solo cambierà il mondo in meglio, ma è anche un modo più facile per cambiarlo.

La Bibbia è chiara che costruiamo la speranza coltivando la nostra relazione con Dio e poi lavorando per aiutare i nostri fratelli e sorelle a costruire quella stessa relazione nelle loro vite. La ragione per cui possiamo sperare non è perché la gente sia così meravigliosa—non bisogna vivere molto a lungo per rendersi conto che non lo è. La ragione per cui speriamo è perché serviamo un Dio stupendo e fedele che cammina con noi attraverso il peggio delle nostre prove.

Ricorda che abbiamo una speranza immeritata

I messaggi di Gesù sul perdono chiariscono che una delle ragioni principali per cui dobbiamo perdonare gli altri è che abbiamo ricevuto un grande e immeritato perdono. Lo stesso vale per la speranza.

Ciascuno di noi era senza speranza e senza motivo per aspettarsi di ricevere speranza eppure ci fu dato un raggio di luce nel mezzo della nostra oscurità. Forse parte del motivo per cui abbiamo tanta difficoltà a sperare cose buone per le persone intorno a noi è che non ricordiamo quanto eravamo senza speranza prima di trovare la grazia.

Se Gesù è stato in grado di portare speranza alla nostra esistenza senza speranza, certamente può fare meraviglie nei cuori e nelle vite degli altri intorno a noi. Le uniche persone su cui dovremmo rassegnarci sono quelle su cui anche il nostro Salvatore si è rassegnato.

I piccoli sforzi fanno la differenza

Ricordo di una conversazione con un giovane che progettava di entrare in medicina e aveva in programma di andare in un paese straniero per servire la gente lì. Mentre parlavamo, un uomo più anziano si intromise e condivise che vedeva poca speranza di cambiamento nei paesi in via di sviluppo.

La gente in quei paesi non era interessata a migliorare e non faceva il minimo necessario per prevenire cose come vermi e parassiti. Medici e infermieri non potevano fare la differenza in un ambiente del genere.

Sentii il cuore del giovane afflosciarsi mentre quell’uomo più anziano parlava. Aveva esperienza e aveva perso la speranza. La cosa triste era che stava anche rubando la speranza di qualcuno che ancora desiderava servire.

Quando ero in formazione, un chirurgo mi disse che i medici di famiglia non facevano davvero niente. Semplicemente mantenevano i pazienti in vita fino alla visita successiva, mentre i chirurghi “aggiustavano” davvero le persone—rimuovendo (o tagliando via) la parte corporea che dava fastidio.

Alla fine della giornata, i piccoli sforzi fanno la differenza. Non faccio neurochirurgia, ma posso comunque fare la differenza nella vita di qualcuno—forse soltanto spendendo un po’ di tempo ad ascoltare e a pregare. Questo vale per tutti noi.

Più di questo, arriviamo a capire che fare questo sforzo cambia in meglio anche le nostre vite. Gesù disse alle pecore che mentre erano al servizio “dei più piccoli di questi miei fratelli” stavano servendo Lui.

Anche se la vita di nessuno migliorasse, il nostro Salvatore conosce i nostri desideri e sente i nostri sforzi, e li ricompenserà un giorno.

Qualche cosa da ricordare

Quando affrontiamo fallimenti, tendiamo a muoverci in una delle due direzioni. Noi ottimisti tendiamo a credere che quell’episodio sia stato un evento isolato e che il futuro sia ancora luminoso. I pessimisti, d’altra parte, credono che i fallimenti siano permanenti, personali e pervasivi.

I pessimisti credono che i loro insuccessi siano il risultato di difetti intrinseci del carattere che possiedono e che queste cose influenzino tutta la loro vita e siano improbabili da cambiare. A differenza dell’uomo giusto che cade per poi rialzarsi, queste persone cadono e restano dove sono cadute, sconfitte fin dall’inizio.

Quando abbiamo a che fare con gli altri, dobbiamo dare loro la stessa grazia che dovremmo concedere a noi stessi. Anche loro stanno crescendo, e se oggi hanno un fallimento, domani faranno meglio. Forse falliranno di nuovo, ma almeno “falliranno meglio.”

Conclusione

Il cinismo è diffuso nel nostro mondo. Molti hanno perso la speranza in un futuro migliore, ed è comprensibile per coloro che hanno riposto la loro speranza nelle istituzioni di questo mondo. Non c’è una vera speranza nel governo, negli eserciti o nella burocrazia.

La canzone dice: “Oh to have no hope in Jesus, how dark this world must be!” Perché Gesù è colui che porta luce nella nostra oscurità e ci permette di andare avanti, anche quando gli altri ci deludono.

Dio è colui che ci redime. È colui che mandò i profeti, anche se i loro messaggi furono ignorati e i profeti perseguitati. È colui che continua a sperare per noi, anche quando Lo abbiamo deluso tante volte in passato.

Lui è la ragione per cui andiamo avanti. Lui è la ragione per cui abbiamo speranza, non solo per noi stessi ma anche per i nostri fratelli.

Eight-year-old Jamin wasn’t very smart. Or at least that’s what his older brother told him. Almost daily, brother Kenny found ways to remind Jamin of his shortcomings and laugh at his blunders.

“Jamin, you will never be smart”, Kenny said. Deep inside Jamin felt resigned to a life of muddled trip-ups. Would he always be clumsy? Would he always say things wrong? That’s what Kenny said.

Jamin believed Kenny’s lectures with wide-eyed belief. Kenny was three years older than him, so he must be right. Very well, then Jamin would be simple. Kenny would be smart. Life was not fair. Dad and Mom disliked Kenny’s proud talk and punished him whenever they walked in on one of his speeches. But Kenny had a way of avoiding earshot. So he continued mocking Jamin.

Grandma Otto watched these trials from her rocker on the porch. She was a quiet old lady.

“Jamin, do you know where Kenny is?” Mom asked with a smile. “It’s almost supper time.”

“He went to check his coyote traps. I’ll go find him.”

There was a chill in the air as he tramped up over the lawn, and the sun was growing old as he crossed the border of the woods. The fleeting shadows scurried over the hills. The chill deepened as he stumped further in. He breathed the rich air and followed Kenny’s trail. Eventually, the trail would end up in a meadow, but Jamin hoped he would find Kenny before he had to go that far. The various traps had been checked already, so Jamin knew Kenny had come this way. Jamin trudged on resolutely. His golden head caught the tired beams that fled from the sun as they flickered through the trees. And soon those too had faded leaving behind the musky smell of the woods. The fall webworms had been at work, and their web curtains shuttered from branches overhead.

At length, as the trees subdued and thinned, and the meadow appeared Jamin knew this was the end of his brother’s trap route. If Kenny wasn’t here, he wouldn’t know where else to look.

But Kenny was there. As Jamin clumped into the meadow, he could see a frustrated heap to his right. The heap’s voice had a familiar ring. The heap’s face was lit in pain. The heap was Kenny. “Are you alright? What happened?” Jamin felt strange, seeing Kenny scrunched in the dirt. Kenny was smart. “Did you step in a trap?”

“Yes, Jamin. I..I wasn’t looking where I was going. Help me. Please.”

Jamin bent and found an ankle firmly held in the jaws of a steel trap. Darkness stained the ground around Kenny. Quickly, Jamin’s strong arms pried open the jaws. Kenny reeled free. “Can you walk?”

“Yes. I think so. If you support me, I can hobble along.”

“Dad and Mom will be worried. We’ve missed supper.”

Sure enough, as the brothers hobbled back through the woods, they heard the long calling of their father. Jamin called back, and he was by their side in a moment, seeing the ankle and scooping up Kenny like a hurt sheep. The odd little band hurried home, and the screen door banged shut as Dad swept across the porch. Jamin went to the wash house and scrubbed his hands. He headed for the front door.

“Jamin.” It was Grandma. The porch light showed her in her old rocker. A heavy comforter lay on her shoulders.

“Yes, Grandma?”

“Do you think you are not very smart?”

“That’s what Kenny says.” Jamin squirmed.

“You were strong enough to open the trap, and Kenny wasn’t. You were brave enough to find him in the dark. Lots of young boys wouldn’t be.” Jamin was silent. Grandma Otto rocked some more, then smiled. “God made you the way you are for a reason, Jamin. He made Kenny the way he is for a reason. He has a plan for you, and a place only you can fill, you know.”

Jamin turned and walked into the warm kitchen. He was smiling.

Åtte år gamle Jamin var ikke særlig smart. Eller i det minste var det det storebroren hans sa til ham. Nesten hver dag fant broren Kenny måter å minne Jamin om hans mangler og le av tabbene hans.

«Jamin, du kommer aldri til å bli smart», sa Kenny. Dypt inne i Jamin følte han seg resignert til et liv fylt av forviklinger. Kom han alltid til å være klosset? Kom han alltid til å si ting feil? Det var i alle fall det Kenny sa.

Jamin trodde på Kennys formaninger med vidåpne øyne. Kenny var tre år eldre enn ham, så han måtte ha rett. Greit, da skulle Jamin være enkel. Kenny skulle være smart. Livet var ikke rettferdig. Far og Mor likte ikke Kennys stolte snakk og straffet ham når de kom inn på en av hans taler. Men Kenny hadde en måte å unngå å bli hørt på. Så han fortsatte å gjøre narr av Jamin.

Bestemor Otto så disse prøvelsene fra gyngestolen på verandaen. Hun var en stille gammel dame.

«Jamin, vet du hvor Kenny er?» spurte Mor med et smil. «Det er nesten tid for middag.»

«Han dro for å sjekke coyotefellene sine. Jeg skal gå og finne ham.»

Det var en kjølig luft da han trampet over plenen, og solen var blitt gammel da han krysset grensen til skogen. De flyktige skyggene skyndte seg over åsene. Kulden dypet seg mens han gikk lenger inn. Han pustet inn den rike luften og fulgte Kennys spor. Etter hvert ville stien ende i en eng, men Jamin håpet han skulle finne Kenny før han måtte gå så langt. De ulike fellene var allerede sjekket, så Jamin visste at Kenny hadde gått denne veien. Jamin trasket videre bestemt. Hans gyldne hode fanget de trette solstrålene som slapp gjennom trærne. Og snart hadde også de falmet, og etterlot seg skogenes jordaktige duft. Etterhvert hadde nettspinnerne vært i arbeid, og deres nettgardiner hang fra greinene over hodet.

Etter hvert, da trærne stilnet og tynnet ut, og engen dukket opp, visste Jamin at dette var slutten på brorens fellrute. Hvis Kenny ikke var her, visste han ikke hvor annet å lete.

Men Kenny var der. Da Jamin trådte inn i enga, kunne han se en frustrert haug til høyre for seg. Haugens stemme hadde en velkjent klang. Haugens ansikt var opplyst av smerte. Haugen var Kenny. «Er du ok? Hva skjedde?» Jamin følte det merkelig å se Kenny sammenkrøpet i jordet. Kenny var smart. «Tråkket du i en felle?»

«Ja, Jamin. Jeg… jeg så ikke hvor jeg gikk. Hjelp meg. Vær så snill.»

Jamin bøyde seg og fant en ankel fast holdt i kjevene på en stålfelle. Mørket farget bakken rundt Kenny. Raskt vred Jamins sterke armer opp kjevene. Kenny slynget seg fri. «Kan du gå?»

«Ja. Jeg tror det. Hvis du støtter meg, kan jeg halte videre.»

«Far og Mor vil være bekymret. Vi har gått glipp av middagen.»

Jo, da — mens brødrene haltet tilbake gjennom skogen, hørte de farens lange rop. Jamin ropte tilbake, og han var ved deres side på et øyeblikk, så ankelen og løftet Kenny opp som et skadet lam. Den merkelige lille gruppen skyndte seg hjem, og dørskjermen smalt igjen idet Far hastet over verandaen. Jamin gikk til vaskerommet og skrubbet hendene sine. Han gikk mot inngangsdøren.

«Jamin.» Det var Bestemor. Verandalampen viste henne i den gamle gyngestolen. Et tungt teppe lå over skuldrene hennes.

«Ja, Bestemor?»

«Tror du at du ikke er særlig smart?»

«Det er det Kenny sier.» Jamin vred seg.

«Du var sterk nok til å åpne fellen, og Kenny var det ikke. Du var modig nok til å finne ham i mørket. Mange unge gutter ville ikke vært det.» Jamin var taus. Bestemor Otto gynget litt mer, så smilte hun. «Gud gjorde deg slik du er av en grunn, Jamin. Han gjorde Kenny slik han er av en grunn. Han har en plan for deg, og et sted bare du kan fylle, vet du.»

Jamin snudde seg og gikk inn i det varme kjøkkenet. Han smilte.

I can still smell the tantalizing cacophony of odors as I clutched my father’s strong hand, weaving our way through the masses of tourists that crowded the building. The vendors at the Green Dragon Farmer’s Market in Ephrata, PA, were trying their best to entice buyers with their rows of fresh fish over ice, cheeses of every variety, deli meat and sandwiches, and piles of fresh fruit. And, oh, the candy! My young preschool mind had never seen so many delectable sweets in one place at one time.

The past two days for me were like the boy at the candy store. I had the privilege of attending Christian Aid Ministries’ first Annual Writers’ Conference. I brushed shoulders with well-known authors such as Katrina Hoover Lee, Johnny Miller, and Ruthann Stelfox. I chatted with aspiring writers and seasoned school teachers. I had the opportunity to sit under hours of inspirational and educational workshops on how to write to communicate, using realistic dialog, descriptive writing, and much more. We all had one common goal in mind. Together, we share and learn how to effectively communicate what is in our hearts, and through the power of the written word, transmit those thoughts to your hearts.

The Heartbeat of the Remnant is a means to communicate inspirational thoughts to eager readers scattered across the globe. Courageous writers step forward with pen and paper or keyboard and monitor and help spread the Good News of the Word of God with caution, correction, and edification. Yet, we need more such writers. We need young believers who bravely submit their first children’s stories. Seasoned grandfathers who bring words of admonishment to the younger generation. Mothers who share experiences and trials with other mothers who are in the throes of raising little ones. Youth encouraging fellow youth to press toward the mark of the prize of the high calling in Christ Jesus. Fathers who with a concerned eye watch the world pressing in on the Christian homes. Together, these aspiring writers will produce a periodical that will endure on the family coffee table for many years. I encourage you, fellow believers, to give it a try. Nelson Mandela, former president of South Africa wrote, “Failure is a teacher, and at the end of your life, what do you think you’ll feel worst about, failing or never trying?”

In 2017 and 2018, the Berean Voice printed a series of vaccine articles in The Heartbeat of the Remnant magazine. These articles were a sincere effort to examine various aspects of vaccine usage with an unbiased approach. We attempted to present the facts as clearly as possible and let the readers draw their own conclusions.

Since then, we have received numerous requests from our readers to publish all the vaccine articles in a booklet, which we agreed to do. But then along came 2019, bringing coronavirus with it. This monumental event upended the vaccine debate and ushered in a frenzied rush to market COVID-19 remedies, many of which were not properly tested. We put the printing on hold, unsure whether to include information on these new and unproven COVID-19 “vaccines.” As time progressed and the deadly nature of COVID-19 abated, we decided to publish the original vaccine articles in a booklet without any additional articles on the COVID-19 debate. We are pleased that the project is nearing completion and will be announced when it is released.

Blessings to all,

Edward Martin

گزشتہ دو دن میرے لیے مٹھائی کی دکان میں کھڑے لڑکے کی مانند تھے۔ مجھے کرسچن ایڈ مینز کے پہلے سالانہ ادیبوں کے کانفرنس میں شرکت کا شرف حاصل ہوا۔ میں نے کیٹرینا ہوور لی، جانی ملر، اور رتھان اسٹیل فاکس جیسے معروف مصنفین کے ساتھ کندھے ملائے۔ میں نے اُمّید مند لکھاریوں اور تجربہ کار اسکول اساتذہ سے باتیں کیں۔ مجھے ایسے حوصلہ افزا اور تعلیمی ورکشاپس سُننے کا موقع ملا جو یہ سکھاتے تھے کہ مؤثر انداز میں کیسے لکھا جائے، حقیقت پسندانہ مکالمے، تفصیلی تحریر، اور بہت کچھ۔ ہمارا ایک مشترکہ مقصد تھا۔ ہم سب مل کر اپنی دل کی باتیں بانٹتے اور سیکھتے ہیں کہ کس طرح تحریر کی قوت کے ذریعے وہ خیالات آپ کے دلوں تک پہنچائے جائیں۔

The Heartbeat of the Remnant مشتاق قارئین تک متاثر کن خیالات پہنچانے کا ذریعہ ہے جو دنیا بھر میں بکھرے ہوئے ہیں۔ دلیر لکھاری قلم و کاغذ یا کی بورڈ اور مانیٹر کے ساتھ آگے آتے ہیں اور خدا کے کلام کی خوشخبری کو احتیاط، اصلاح، اور تعمیر کے ساتھ پھیلانے میں مدد کرتے ہیں۔ پھر بھی، ہمیں ایسے مزید لکھاریوں کی ضرورت ہے۔ ہمیں نوجوان مومنین کی ضرورت ہے جو بہادری سے اپنے پہلے بچوں کی کہانیاں پیش کریں۔ تجربہ کار دادا جو نوجوان نسل کو نصیحت کے الفاظ دیں۔ مائیں جو اپنے تجربات اور آزمائشیں دیگر ماؤں کے ساتھ بانٹیں جو ننھے بچوں کی پرورش میں مصروف ہیں۔ نوجوان ایک دوسرے کو مسیح یسوع میں اعلیٰ پکار کے انعام کی نشان تک پہنچنے کی طرف بڑھنے کی ترغیب دیں۔ باپ جو فکر مند نگاہ کے ساتھ مسیحی گھروں پر دنیا کے دباؤ کو دیکھتے ہیں۔ مل کر، یہ اُمّید مند لکھاری ایک ایسی رسالہ تیار کریں گے جو کئی سالوں تک گھر کی کافی ٹیبل پر برقرار رہے گی۔ میں آپ سب مومنین کی حوصلہ افزائی کرتا ہوں کہ ایک بار کوشش کریں۔ جنوبی افریقہ کے سابق صدر نیلسن منڈیلا نے لکھا، “ناکامی ایک استاد ہے، اور آپ کی زندگی کے اختتام پر، آپ کو کیا لگتا ہے کہ آپ کو سب سے زیادہ برا کیا محسوس ہوگا، ناکام ہونا یا کبھی کوشش نہ کرنا؟”

تمام کو برکتیں،

Edward Martin
